title: The relationship between sleep quality, recovery state and musculoskeletal health in professional and semi-professionel German handball players
summary:
Background:
Sleep is important for athletes' health and performance. However, many handball players report experiencing stress and feeling tired, as well as physical discomfort. These factors can negatively affect sleep quality, and similarly, impaired sleep can exacerbate these issues.
Research Question:
Does sleep quality, and the level of recovery and stress, affect how it is linked to physical complaints?
Methodology:
Participants complete a one-time, anonymous online questionnaire. It includes simple questions about their sleep, their feelings of recovery and stress, and any physical discomfort in different parts of the body. Completing the questionnaire takes about 15 to 20 minutes. No physical examinations are carried out. Participation is voluntary and can be ended at any time without giving a reason. All answers are anonymous and are evaluated only in summarized form to examine possible connections between sleep, recovery, stress, and physical complaints.
conditions: Musculoskeletal complaints as well as impaired sleep quality and recovery–stress state in handball players.

interventions.name:
Professional and semi-professional handball players
Participants complete a one-time online questionnaire.
The assessment includes the following validated instruments:
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) to assess sleep quality
RESTQ-Sport to measure recovery and stress state

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Aged between 18 and 35 to ensure a homogeneous sample.
Voluntary participation in the study.
Providing informed consent (declaration of consent).
Professional or semi-professional handball players who have trained regularly in the last month.
Exclusion criteria:
Lack of consent to participate in the study.
Severe acute or chronic illnesses that have prevented regular training in the last month.
Injuries requiring long-term rehabilitation, such as ligament injuries requiring surgery, fractures, persistent or chronic musculoskeletal pain, existing diagnosed sleep disorders, in particular: severe insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, and the use of medications specifically used to treat these disorders.
